title: Area VIII review: Basic Instrument Maneuvers
intro: These questions mix all six Tasks of Area VIII: level flight, climbs, descents and turns by instruments, unusual attitude recovery, and radios and navigation. Many join two Tasks in one scenario.

questions.q: You are flying at 130 knots true airspeed on a heading of 270°. ATC says, "Turn left heading 180." Using the IFH rules of thumb for a standard rate turn, about what bank do you use, and when do you start the roll-out?
options: About 13° of bank; start the roll-out at about 187°
About 30° of bank; start the roll-out at about 195°
About 20° of bank; start the roll-out at about 170°
About 20° of bank; start the roll-out at about 190°
questions.why: Standard rate bank is about the airspeed divided by 10, plus half of that: 13 + 6.5 = 19.5, so about 20°. Lead the roll-out by half the bank, about 10° [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. In a left turn the heading numbers go down, so start rolling out at about 190°.

questions.q: In straight-and-level cruise, the altimeter is holding steady right on 4,500 feet, but the airspeed is 8 knots below your planned cruise speed. What is the best fix?
options: Add a little power, since the altitude is already right
Raise the nose a little and hold it to pick up the lost speed
Retrim nose-down and leave the power alone to regain speed
Lower the nose a little to gain speed, then climb back to 4,500
questions.why: At a constant altitude, power sets the airspeed. Always check the altimeter before deciding a power change is needed [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. Pushing forward for low airspeed when the real cause is low power is a common error [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]; it would cost you altitude.

questions.q: Your CFI sets up this attitude while your eyes are closed, then says "Recover." With no recovery procedure in your POH, what is the full sequence of control inputs?
options: Reduce power, level the wings, then apply back pressure to raise the nose
Level the wings first, then add power and apply forward pressure to lower the nose
Add power, apply forward pressure to lower the nose, then level the wings
Apply forward pressure to lower the nose, reduce power, then level the wings
questions.why: Airspeed decreasing and altitude increasing in a right bank means nose-high. Add power in proportion to the slowing, apply forward pressure to lower the nose and prevent a stall, then level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder. Do them almost at once, but in that order [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. Reduce power, level, raise is the nose-low order.

questions.q: Under the hood with flight following, your heading indicator fails, and you tell Approach. Instead of headings, what kind of vectors can the controller give you?
options: Magnetic compass headings only, which you must hold within 5°
"Turn right," "turn left" and "stop turn," while watching your track on radar
Names of GPS waypoints to fly direct to
A number of seconds to turn, for a timed turn
questions.why: This is a no-gyro vector. The controller watches your radar track and says "turn right" or "turn left" and "stop turn" instead of giving headings [[34:385|AIM P/C Glossary]]. Make each turn at standard rate, and start it as soon as you hear the call [[33:431|AIM 5-4-11]].

questions.q: You raise the nose to the climb attitude and add full power. The nose keeps rising past the picture you wanted, and the airplane starts to yaw left. What is happening?
options: The attitude indicator is precessing from the power change, so ignore it until the climb is stable and reset it
The airplane is about to stall because the nose is too high, so reduce power right away and lower the nose
Slipstream over the tail raises the nose, and P-factor and torque yaw you left, so hold attitude and add right rudder
Turbulence is lifting the nose and pushing the tail around, so level off and wait for smoother air before continuing
questions.why: In many airplanes, more power means more slipstream over the horizontal tail, so the nose rises more than you want. P-factor and torque roll and yaw the airplane left, so use right rudder and some aileron [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

questions.q: You are descending at 500 fpm to 3,000 feet and want to level off at cruise speed. You added cruise power at 3,120 feet. When do you raise the nose to the level attitude?
options: At about 3,050 feet, holding forward pressure until then
At 3,000 feet exactly
At about 3,150 feet, so the airplane speeds up in level flight
Right away, as soon as the power is in
questions.why: At 500 fpm, add cruise power 100 to 150 feet above the altitude. The nose tends to rise as speed builds, so hold forward pressure to keep the descent going until about 50 feet above, then smoothly raise the nose to level [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

questions.q: In smooth air you are holding 5,500 feet. The altimeter hasn't moved for a minute, but the VSI shows a steady 100 fpm descent. What should you do?
options: Raise the nose until the VSI reads zero
Open the alternate static source, since the static port is blocked
Use the 100 fpm down reading as the zero point for level flight
Add power until the VSI reads zero
questions.why: Some VSIs show a small climb or descent while the airplane is level. If so, use that reading as the zero position [[23:167|IFH 7-6]]. A blocked static port would leave the VSI stuck on zero, not off zero [[23:98|IFH 5-3]].

questions.q: Your heading indicator has failed, and you need to reverse course (turn 180°). Which plan is best?
options: Make a standard rate turn for 2 minutes, starting as the second hand passes a cardinal point, then check the compass once level
Roll into a 30° bank and roll out when the magnetic compass shows the new heading, correcting for compass lag
Make a standard rate turn for 90 seconds, starting as the second hand passes a cardinal point, then check the compass once level
Make a standard rate turn for 60 seconds, starting as the second hand passes a cardinal point, then check the compass
questions.why: At 3° per second, 180° takes 60 seconds. Start the roll-in as the second hand passes a cardinal point, roll out when the time is up, then check the turn with the compass [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. Past about 18° of bank the compass is erratic [[23:106|IFH 5-11]], so turning steeply by the compass is a poor plan.

questions.q: Your autopilot suddenly rolls the airplane into a steep bank, and the nose starts to drop. You disconnect the autopilot. Following the AFH upset recovery template, what do you do next?
options: Pull back firmly to stop the descent
Apply forward pressure to unload, then roll the wings to the nearest horizon
Roll the wings level toward the farthest horizon
Reduce power to idle and wait for the speed to settle
questions.why: The template: 1. disconnect the wing leveler or autopilot, 2. apply forward pressure to unload, 3. roll the wings to the nearest horizon, 4. adjust power by watching airspeed, 5. return to level flight [[24:111|AFH 5-6]].

questions.q: On a very cold winter day, you descend to 2,500 feet indicated over hills with the correct altimeter setting. Compared with what the altimeter shows, where is the airplane really?
options: Lower than indicated
Higher than indicated
Exactly as indicated, since the setting is correct
Lower than indicated only if the static port is blocked
questions.why: When the air is colder than standard, your true altitude is lower than indicated, even with the right altimeter setting [[23:100|IFH 5-5]]. Allow extra room above terrain.

questions.q: You check in with Approach as "Cessna One Two Three Four Five." When may you start calling yourself "Cessna Three Four Five"?
options: Right away on the first call, as long as no similar call sign is on the frequency
After the controller shortens it first, if no similar call sign is on the frequency
Only after you reach your cruising altitude and the controller has acknowledged your position
Never; you must use the full call sign for the whole flight, even if ATC shortens it first
questions.why: Never shorten your call sign on initial contact or when similar call signs are on the frequency. Once communication is set up, ATC may shorten it to the prefix and the last three characters, and then you may use the short form too [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4]].

questions.q: Your attitude indicator shows the nose two bar widths up at full power. A jet pilot sets the exact same picture on the attitude indicator. What does the IFH say about the results?
options: Both airplanes climb at the same rate, since the picture on the attitude indicator is the same
The results differ a lot, because performance comes from attitude plus power
Both airplanes climb at the same airspeed, since the attitude indicator picture is the same
The jet climbs more slowly, since it is heavier and needs a higher nose attitude
questions.why: In the IFH example, the small airplane climbs 500 fpm at 90 knots, while the jet with the same picture climbs 2,000 fpm at 250 knots. Attitude plus power equals performance, so learn the pictures for your own airplane [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].

questions.q: As a VFR pilot you flew into cloud, and ATC helped you get out. You break out into clear air at dusk near an airport you don't know, and you feel strong pressure to land right away. What does the AFH advise?
options: Land at once, before the weather closes in again, on the first runway you can see even if you are not set up for it
Fly a low, tight pattern so you never lose sight of the runway, and land on the first approach you set up
Climb back into the cloud and hold there until ATC clears you, rather than trying to land at an unfamiliar airport
Take time to adjust and get oriented first, even if that means flying straight and level or circling the airport
questions.why: An untrained pilot often feels self-imposed pressure to get on the ground. If possible, allow time to adjust and get oriented before the approach and landing, even if it means flying straight and level for a time or circling the airport, especially at night [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

questions.q: After each turn to a heading, you end up 80 to 100 feet above your altitude. What is the most likely cause?
options: Rolling out too early
Using too little back pressure on the roll-in
Not lowering the nose as the bank comes off during the roll-out
Not adding power on the roll-in
questions.why: As you roll out, the vertical part of lift grows. If you don't lower the pitch to match, you gain altitude after every turn [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. Too little back pressure on the roll-in does the opposite: it loses altitude.

questions.q: Descending through rain, you notice the altimeter is frozen and the VSI reads zero. You open the alternate static source inside the cabin. What should the instruments show now?
options: Altimeter and VSI work again, but the airspeed reads zero until you descend
Altimeter a little low, airspeed low, and a brief descent on the VSI, then steady
All three instruments read exactly right again, with no error from the cabin pressure
Altimeter a little high, airspeed a little high, and a brief climb on the VSI
questions.why: A frozen altimeter and a VSI stuck on zero mean a blocked static system. Cabin air pressure is lower than outside, so on alternate static the altimeter reads slightly high, the airspeed reads high, and the VSI shows a momentary climb [[23:98|IFH 5-3]].

questions.q: In haze with no horizon, you pull the throttle back quickly to start a descent. What false feeling can this cause, and what is the danger?
options: A nose-up feeling, so you may push the nose down into a steep dive
A turning feeling, so you may roll the other way and enter a spiral
No false feeling at all, since a power change in level flight is too small to notice
A nose-down feeling, so you may pull back hard toward a stall
questions.why: This is the somatogravic illusion. Quick acceleration feels like nose-up. A quick power reduction has the opposite effect, and a disoriented pilot may pull into a nose-up or stall attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. The PHAK defines it as a false sense of a nose-up or nose-down attitude from a rapid acceleration or deceleration [[1:503|PHAK Glossary G-27]]. Reduce power smoothly and fly the attitude indicator.

questions.q: You have flight following in haze over hills. Approach has said "radar contact" and now tells you to descend to an altitude that seems too low for the hills ahead. What should you do?
options: Descend right away, since radar contact means ATC is handling your terrain clearance for you
Ask the controller about the altitude before you descend, since terrain clearance is still yours
Descend as assigned, but squawk 7700 first so ATC watches you closely on the way down
Stay where you are and say nothing, since ATC will cancel the descent if it is unsafe for terrain
questions.why: If an assigned altitude seems too low, ask the controller before descending [[23:57|IFH 2-6]]. Hearing "radar contact" doesn't relieve you of terrain clearance [[23:58|IFH 2-7]]. For a VFR pilot, ATC help is advisory, and flying safely stays your job [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17]].

questions.q: During a climb in visible moisture, the airspeed kept rising even though your attitude and power didn't change. You suspect the pitot tube and its drain hole are blocked. If you now descend, what will the airspeed indicator show?
options: An increasing airspeed, because the blocked pitot holds the pressure from the climb
A steady and correct airspeed, since the static port is still open to the outside air
Zero right away, since no ram air reaches the instrument at all
A decreasing airspeed, even if your real speed stays the same
questions.why: With the pitot tube and drain hole blocked, the airspeed indicator acts like an altimeter [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]. In a climb it shows more airspeed; in a descent, the rising static pressure makes it show less [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].

questions.q: In cloud, you hold a steady standard rate turn for 30 seconds. Partway through, it starts to feel like level flight. Why?
options: The fluid in your inner ear has caught up with the turn, which takes about 15 to 20 seconds, so you no longer sense it
Your body is right: the turn has stopped on its own
The haze is creating a false horizon
The turn coordinator has drifted back to level
questions.why: Friction makes the fluid in the inner ear take about 15 to 20 seconds to match the motion of the canal [[23:71|IFH 3-4]]. In a steady turn you then feel no turn, and when you roll out you may feel a turn the other way [[23:72|IFH 3-5]]. Trust the instruments.

questions.q: You are holding straight and level under the hood. The altimeter starts unwinding much faster than it ever does in normal level flight. What does the IFH say to do first?
options: Assume an unusual attitude and speed up your cross-check to see what is happening
Wait a few seconds without changing your scan, so the VSI can confirm the descent first
Tap the altimeter lightly, since it is probably sticking, and keep flying by its reading
Pull back right away to stop the descent before you work out what the instruments are doing
questions.why: Any time an instrument moves at a rate or shows a reading that doesn't fit the maneuver, assume an unusual attitude and speed up the cross-check to tell an attitude problem from an instrument error or failure [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. Pulling back before you know the bank can tighten a spiral and lose even more altitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

questions.q: Approach says, "Cessna Three Four Five, ident." What do you do?
options: Change your transponder code to 1200 and tell the controller when it has changed
Hold the IDENT button down until ATC says radar contact, so the target stays highlighted
Press the IDENT button briefly, so your target stands out on the controller's screen
Read back your call sign and altitude only, since ident does not call for any transponder action
questions.why: When asked to ident, briefly push the IDENT button. It brightens your return on the controller's scope so they can identify you [[23:54|IFH 2-3]].

questions.q: Before a hood lesson, you set the current altimeter setting on the ramp. The field elevation is 1,240 feet, and the altimeter reads 1,340 feet. What should you do?
options: Have the altimeter checked by a repair station, since it is off by more than 75 feet
Subtract 100 feet from every reading in flight
Fly; anything within 200 feet is fine
Fly, but use the VSI instead of the altimeter
questions.why: With the current setting, the altimeter should show the field elevation. If it is off by more than 75 feet, it should go to a certificated instrument repair station [[23:100|IFH 5-5]]. Here it is off by 100 feet (1,340 - 1,240).

questions.q: You are VFR, not instrument rated, and have lost the horizon in haze. To clear a ridge, you raised the nose one bar width and added some power, but the climb rate is too low. What does the AFH suggest next?
options: Raise the nose another two bar widths to climb faster, accepting a lower airspeed to clear the ridge
Add power in small steps of about 100 rpm or 1 inch of manifold pressure until the climb is enough
Make a steep climbing turn away from the ridge to gain altitude faster, then turn back on course
Pitch for best angle of climb speed and hold that airspeed exactly, adding power only if needed
questions.why: Raise the nose no more than one bar width, add power, and accept whatever airspeed results. If the climb rate is too low, add power in steps of 100 rpm or 1 inch of manifold pressure [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]. Untrained pilots should avoid climbing turns [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

questions.q: In a constant airspeed descent your speed is a bit high, so you plan to raise the nose. On the attitude indicator, one bar width (the wings and center dot of the miniature airplane) stands for about how much pitch?
options: About 10°
About 5°
About 2°
About 15°
questions.why: The wings and center dot of the miniature airplane, one bar width, stand for about 2° of pitch [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]. Pitch changes should not be more than half a bar width at a time [[23:138|IFH 6-5]].
